questions.q: A current of 0.25 A flows in a wire for 2.0 minutes. How much charge passes a point in the wire?
questions.solution: The time must be in seconds: 2.0 × 60 = 120 s. Then \(Q = It\) = 0.25 × 120 = 30 C. A common slip is to leave the time in minutes (0.50 C).

questions.q: A 12 V battery moves 5.0 C of charge around a circuit. How much energy does the battery transfer to the charge?
questions.solution: Potential difference is the energy transferred per unit charge, \(V = \frac{W}{Q}\). So \(W = QV\) = 5.0 × 12 = 60 J.

questions.q: A current of 3.2 mA flows for 10 s. How many electrons pass a point in that time? (\(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\))
questions.solution: Charge: \(Q = It = 3.2 \times 10^{-3} \times 10 = 0.032\ \text{C}\). Number of electrons: \(\frac{Q}{e} = \frac{0.032}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 2.0 \times 10^{17}\). Leaving the current in mA gives \(10^{20}\); leaving out the time gives \(10^{16}\).

questions.q: Which is a correct statement of Ohm's law?

options.A: The current in a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the temperature stays constant.
options.B: The resistance of a conductor is its potential difference divided by its current.
options.C: The resistance of a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it.
options.D: The current in a conductor is inversely proportional to the potential difference across it.

questions.solution: Ohm's law says that current is directly proportional to potential difference when physical conditions such as temperature are constant. \(R = \frac{V}{I}\) is the definition of resistance: it is true for every component, ohmic or not, so it is not Ohm's law.

questions.q: Current (y-axis) is plotted against potential difference (x-axis) for a filament lamp. Which describes the graph for positive values?

options.A: A curve through the origin whose gradient decreases as the potential difference increases.
options.B: A straight line through the origin.
options.C: A curve through the origin whose gradient increases as the potential difference increases.
options.D: Almost zero current at first, then a steep rise.

questions.solution: A larger current heats the filament, so its metal ions vibrate more and its resistance rises. Each extra volt then adds less current, so the curve gets flatter. A straight line is an ohmic conductor; a steep rise after a threshold is a diode.

questions.q: The potential difference across a silicon diode in forward bias is raised slowly from zero. Which describes the current?

options.A: Almost zero until about 0.6 V, then it rises steeply.
options.B: Directly proportional to the potential difference.
options.C: It rises steeply at first, then levels off.
options.D: Almost zero at every potential difference.

questions.solution: A diode conducts in forward bias only once the potential difference passes its threshold, about 0.6 V for silicon. Beyond that its resistance falls sharply and the current rises steeply. Almost zero current at every value describes reverse bias.

questions.q: A wire is 2.0 m long with a cross-sectional area of \(1.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{2}\). Its material has a resistivity of \(1.1 \times 10^{-6}\ \Omega\ \text{m}\). What is the resistance of the wire?
questions.solution: \(R = \frac{\rho l}{A} = \frac{1.1 \times 10^{-6} \times 2.0}{1.0 \times 10^{-7}} = 22\ \Omega\). Common slips: leaving out the length (\(11\ \Omega\)), or dividing by it (\(5.5\ \Omega\)).

questions.q: A wire has resistance \(R\). A second wire of the same material and length has twice the diameter. What is the resistance of the second wire?
questions.solution: \(R = \frac{\rho l}{A}\), and the area depends on the diameter squared. Twice the diameter means four times the area, so the resistance is a quarter of \(R\). Half of \(R\) comes from forgetting to square the diameter.

questions.q: A \(6.0\ \Omega\) resistor and a \(3.0\ \Omega\) resistor are connected in parallel. This pair is connected in series with a \(4.0\ \Omega\) resistor. What is the total resistance?
questions.solution: Parallel pair: \(\frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{6.0} + \frac{1}{3.0} = \frac{1}{2.0}\), which is \(2.0\ \Omega\). Adding the series resistor: total = 2.0 + 4.0 = \(6.0\ \Omega\). Treating all three as in series (\(13\ \Omega\)) ignores the parallel pair.

questions.q: A kettle is rated at 2.0 kW when connected to a 230 V supply. What is the current in the kettle?
questions.solution: \(P = VI\), with the power in watts: 2.0 kW = 2000 W. So \(I = \frac{P}{V}\) = 2000 ÷ 230 = 8.7 A. A common slip is to divide the other way round (0.12 A).

questions.q: A potential difference of 12 V is applied across an \(8.0\ \Omega\) resistor. What power is dissipated in the resistor?
questions.solution: \(P = \frac{V^{2}}{R} = \frac{12^{2}}{8.0} = \frac{144}{8.0}\) = 18 W. The value 1.5 is the current in amps, not the power.

questions.q: Currents of 2.0 A and 3.5 A flow into a junction. Two wires carry current away from it, and one of them carries 1.5 A. What is the current in the other?
questions.solution: Charge is conserved, so the current into a junction equals the current out of it. Current in: 2.0 + 3.5 = 5.5 A. The other wire carries 5.5 − 1.5 = 4.0 A.

questions.q: A \(2.0\ \text{k}\Omega\) resistor and a \(4.0\ \text{k}\Omega\) resistor are connected in series across a 9.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. What is the potential difference across the \(4.0\ \text{k}\Omega\) resistor?
questions.solution: The potential difference divides in the ratio of the resistances: \(V = 9.0 \times \frac{4.0}{2.0 + 4.0}\) = 6.0 V. The value 3.0 V is across the other resistor.

questions.q: An NTC thermistor and a fixed resistor are connected in series across a battery. The temperature of the thermistor rises. What happens to the potential difference across the fixed resistor?

options.A: It increases, because the thermistor's resistance falls.
options.B: It decreases, because the thermistor's resistance falls.
options.C: It increases, because the thermistor's resistance rises.
options.D: It stays the same, because the fixed resistor does not change.

questions.solution: The resistance of an NTC thermistor falls as it gets hotter. The thermistor then takes a smaller share of the battery's potential difference, so the fixed resistor takes a larger share. The current also rises, and \(V = IR\) for the fixed resistor rises with it.

questions.q: A cell of e.m.f. 6.0 V and internal resistance \(1.0\ \Omega\) is connected to a \(5.0\ \Omega\) resistor. What is the potential difference across the terminals of the cell?
questions.solution: Current: \(I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R + r} = \frac{6.0}{5.0 + 1.0}\) = 1.0 A. Terminal potential difference: \(V = IR\) = 1.0 × 5.0 = 5.0 V. The other 1.0 V is the lost volts across the internal resistance.

questions.q: Which is the correct definition of the electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a cell?

options.A: The force that pushes each electron around the circuit.
options.B: The potential difference across the internal resistance of the cell.
options.C: The energy transferred to heat in the cell per unit charge.
options.D: The energy the cell transfers to electrical energy per unit charge passing through it.

questions.solution: E.m.f. is the energy transferred from chemical to electrical energy per unit charge that passes through the cell: \(\varepsilon = \frac{E}{Q}\). Despite its name it is not a force; it is measured in volts.

questions.q: The terminal potential difference \(V\) of a cell (y-axis) is plotted against the current \(I\) in it (x-axis). The cell has e.m.f. \(\varepsilon\) and internal resistance \(r\). What are the gradient and the y-intercept of the straight line?
questions.solution: \(\varepsilon = V + Ir\), so \(V = -rI + \varepsilon\). Comparing with \(y = mx + c\): the gradient is \(-r\) and the intercept is \(\varepsilon\). The line slopes down because more current means more lost volts.

questions.q: A copper wire of cross-sectional area \(1.0 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^{2}\) carries a current of 2.0 A. Copper has \(8.5 \times 10^{28}\) free electrons per cubic metre. What is the drift velocity of the electrons? (\(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\))
questions.solution: \(I = nqvA\), so \(v = \frac{I}{nqA} = \frac{2.0}{8.5 \times 10^{28} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.0 \times 10^{-6}} = 1.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\). Drift velocities are tiny, a fraction of a millimetre per second, because there are so many free electrons.

questions.q: Which statement about a superconductor is correct?

options.A: Its resistivity falls steadily to zero as it is heated.
options.B: Its resistivity is zero at every temperature.
options.C: Its resistivity is zero only at exactly its critical temperature.
options.D: Its resistivity is zero at and below its critical temperature.

questions.solution: A superconductor's resistivity drops suddenly to zero when it is cooled to its critical temperature, and stays zero below it. Above the critical temperature it has ordinary resistance. Uses include strong electromagnets and power cables with no energy loss.

questions.q: A lamp has a potential difference of 6.0 V across it and a current of 0.50 A. How much energy does it transfer in 5.0 minutes?
questions.solution: The time in seconds is 5.0 × 60 = 300 s. \(E = VIt\) = 6.0 × 0.50 × 300 = 900 J. A common slip is to leave the time in minutes (15 J).
